units.title: Hello
units.practical: Practical English — checking in at a hotel

notes: Every English sentence needs a verb. With jobs, nationalities and places that verb is usually be.
We use contractions when we speak: I am → I'm.
Use a / an before a job: She's a doctor.

vocab.def: the name your parents chose for you
the number people call you on
vocab.ex: This is my new phone number.

ex.a: Hi! My name is Anna and I'm a student.

ex.text: Good morning. My first name is Sara and my surname is Nazarova. I am twenty-three years old.

speak.p: Introduce yourself: name, city, job or studies.
speak.model: Hi, I'm Ayan. I'm from Almaty and I'm a student.

speak.p: Ask your partner three personal questions.
speak.model: What's your surname? What's your phone number? How old are you?

speak.p: Introduce your partner to the class.
speak.model: This is Dana. She's from Astana and she's a nurse.

rows.label: Short answers
items: Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.
Yes, she is. / No, she isn't.
Yes, they are. / No, they aren't.

notes: In questions, be goes before the person: Is he …? — not He is …?
Never use a contraction in a positive short answer: Yes, I am. ✓   Yes, I'm. ✗
Nationality adjectives always start with a capital letter: Kazakh, Polish, Japanese.

vocab.ex: Madrid is the capital of Spain.

vocab.def: the main city of a country
a place like Italy or Egypt
vocab.ex: How many countries are in Europe?
How many languages do you speak?

ex.a: I'm not Turkish. I'm from Kazakhstan.

ex.text: Hello. I am Marek. I am not English — I am Polish, from Krakow.

speak.p: Ask and answer: Where are you from? Is it a big city?
speak.model: I'm from Shymkent. Yes, it's quite big.

speak.p: Guess your partner's three favourite countries with yes/no questions.
speak.model: Is it in Europe? Is it Italy?

speak.p: Say one true and one false sentence about a country. Partner corrects the false one.
speak.model: Paris is in Spain. — No, it isn't. It's in France.

rows.label: Possessives
items: my, your, his, her, its, our, their

notes: Possessive adjectives never change with plural nouns: my book, my books.
Use an before a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u), a before all other sounds.
his = of a man, her = of a woman. The owner decides the word, not the object.

vocab.def: the white or black surface the teacher writes on

vocab.ex: My laptop is on the desk.

vocab.def: work you do after the lesson

vocab.ex: Open your books at page ten.

vocab.def: you say this when something is not clear
ask about the letters of a word
vocab.ex: How do you spell it? — D-A-N-A.
Work in pairs and compare answers.

ex.q: This is Dana and this is ___ brother.
Is this ___ email address? — Yes, mine.

ex.a: How do you spell your surname?
Sorry, I don't understand. Can you repeat that?

ex.text: Open your books at page fourteen and work in pairs.

speak.p: Point at five things in your room and name them in English.
speak.model: This is my desk. That's a window.

speak.p: Spell your name, your city and your street for your partner.
speak.model: A-L-M-A-T-Y.

speak.p: Ask for help in three different ways.
speak.model: I don't understand. Can you repeat that? How do you spell it?

test.q: ___ you a teacher? — Yes, I am.
This is Ali and that is ___ wife.

units.title: Things
units.practical: Practical English — in a taxi, giving simple directions

notes: Drop a / an in the plural: a key → keys (not a keys).
Nouns ending in consonant + y change to -ies: diary → diaries.
For "always plural" words use These are … and a pair of …

vocab.def: you open a door with it
you keep money and cards in it
you use it in the rain
you need it to travel or enter
you wear them to see better
vocab.ex: My glasses are on the desk.

vocab.def: you listen to music with them
it shows the time on your arm

ex.q: There are twenty ___ (person) in the room.

pairs: you use it in the rain

ex.a: My keys and my wallet are in my bag.

ex.text: Excuse me, is this your umbrella? — No, it isn't. My umbrella is blue.

speak.p: Empty your bag or pockets. Name six things in English.
speak.model: This is a charger. These are my keys.

speak.p: Ask your partner: Have you got a ticket / a tissue / an umbrella?
speak.model: Have you got a charger? — Yes, I have.

speak.p: Describe one object; your partner guesses it.
speak.model: You use it in the rain. — An umbrella!

notes: Adjectives never take an -s: black shoes ✓   blacks shoes ✗
The adjective goes before the noun: a new phone — not a phone new.
very is stronger than quite.

vocab.ex: They live in a big house.
My flat is small but nice.

vocab.def: it costs a lot of money
the colour between black and white
the colour of red and blue together

ex.a: It is a very expensive watch.

ex.instr: Put the adjective in the right place.

ex.a: It's a very beautiful old city.

ex.text: I want the small purple bag, not the big grey one.

speak.p: Describe three things you are wearing (colour + adjective).
speak.model: These are new black jeans.

speak.p: Your city: name two things that are cheap and two that are expensive.
speak.model: Taxis are quite cheap here.

speak.p: Describe a room in your home in five sentences.
speak.model: My kitchen is small but very nice. The walls are white.

notes: Use this / these for things here, that / those for things over there.
The imperative has no subject: Close the door. — not You close the door.
Feelings use be, not have: I'm hungry. ✓   I have hunger. ✗

vocab.def: you need to sleep or rest
you think something bad can happen
you have too much to do
vocab.ex: I'm stressed. I need a holiday.
I'm cold. Close the window, please.

ex.q: I'm ___. Can I have some water?

ex.a: I'm tired and I'm really hungry.

ex.text: I'm not hungry, but I'm very thirsty. Let's find a café.

speak.p: Say how you feel today and why.
speak.model: I'm a bit tired because I worked late.

speak.p: Give your partner five classroom instructions.
speak.model: Stand up. Close the door. Don't look at your phone.

speak.p: Compare two things in the room with this / that.
speak.model: This chair is comfortable, but that one is better.

test.q: There are two ___ (woman) in the office.

pairs: you think something bad can happen
you have too much to do

units.title: Work and study
units.theme: Jobs, verb phrases, telling the time
units.practical: Practical English — ordering in a coffee shop

notes: Add -s after he, she and it: he works, she drives. Nowhere else.
After doesn't the verb loses its -s: she doesn't work, not she doesn't works.
Verbs ending in a consonant + -y change it: study → he studies, carry → she carries.
go and do take -es: he goes, she does.

vocab.ex: I work in a small office.

vocab.def: to learn a subject at school or university
to leave your bed in the morning
vocab.ex: I get up at seven every day.

vocab.def: to come to the end of something

vocab.ex: He drives to work every morning.
They speak Kazakh and Russian at home.

vocab.def: the room or building where people do their job
vocab.ex: Our office is on the third floor.
She is in her first year at university.

ex.a: I get up at seven every day.

a: He doesn't work in a hospital.

ex.a: I work in an office and I study English.

ex.text: My name is Timur. I live in Almaty and I work in a small office. I don't drive — I take the bus.
ex.q: How does Timur go to work?

ex.instr: Say each verb out loud. Which ending do you hear?

speak.p: Say what you do: work or study, and where.
speak.model: I work in an office in Almaty and I study English in the evening.

speak.p: Say two things you don't do on a normal weekday.
speak.model: I don't get up early and I don't drive to work.

speak.p: Talk about someone in your family: what they do and what they don't do.
speak.model: My sister studies at university. She doesn't work yet.

notes: After do or does the verb has no -s: Does she work?, not Does she works?
What do you do? is how you ask about someone's job.
With be there is no do: Are you a teacher?, not Do you are a teacher?
Jobs take a or an: She's a nurse. He's an engineer.

vocab.ex: The doctor works at the clinic.
She is a nurse in a big hospital.

vocab.def: someone who designs or builds machines
someone whose job is to drive
vocab.ex: The bus driver is very friendly.

vocab.def: someone who brings food in a restaurant
vocab.ex: The waiter brings us the menu.

vocab.def: someone who helps customers in a shop
vocab.ex: My cousin is a shop assistant.

vocab.def: someone who works with the law
vocab.ex: We need a lawyer for this.

vocab.def: someone who works with money and numbers
someone who writes for a newspaper or website
vocab.ex: He is a journalist in Almaty.

a: Does he work in a bank?

ex.a: What does your father do? He's an engineer.

ex.text: This is my friend Aigerim. She works in a hospital in Almaty. She isn't a doctor — she's a nurse.

speak.p: Ask your partner three questions about their job or studies.
speak.model: What do you do? Where do you work? Do you like it?

speak.p: Describe what someone in your family does.
speak.model: My father is an engineer. He works in a big company.

speak.p: Say one job you would like and one you would not.
speak.model: I want to be a journalist. I don't want to be an accountant.

notes: What time asks for the clock; when asks for the day or the moment.
Say past up to thirty minutes, then to the next hour: ten past four, ten to five.
o'clock is only for the exact hour: seven o'clock, never seven ten o'clock.
Why is answered with because: Why are you late? Because the bus was slow.

vocab.ex: The lesson starts at six o'clock.
I get up at half past seven.
We leave at a quarter to nine.

ex.q: ___ are you late? Because the bus was slow.
___ do you go to work? By bus.

ex.a: What time does the lesson start?
The lesson starts at a quarter past six.

ex.text: Our classes start at nine o'clock and finish at half past two. We have lunch at midday.

ex.instr: Put each time in the right group.

speak.p: Say what time you get up, start work or study, and finish.
speak.model: I get up at half past six, I start at nine and I finish at six o'clock.

speak.p: Ask your partner about their day using three different question words.
speak.model: What time do you get up? Where do you work? How do you go there?

speak.p: Say one thing you are always late for, and why.
speak.model: I'm always late for the gym because I finish work at six.

test.a: My sister works in an office.

units.title: Every day
units.practical: Practical English — small talk about your day

rows.label: In sentences
items: My mother teaches at a school.
Aigerim doesn't live with her parents.

notes: The -s belongs to he, she and it and to nobody else.
have is the odd one out: he has, never he haves.
After does and doesn't the -s is already used up: Does she work?, He doesn't watch TV.
To say whose family it is, add 's: my sister's husband, Timur's parents.

vocab.def: a boy or man with the same parents as you
vocab.ex: My brother works at the airport.

vocab.def: a girl or woman with the same parents as you
vocab.ex: Her sister has a small shop.
Their son is six years old.
My daughter starts school in September.

vocab.def: the man a woman is married to
the woman a man is married to
the mother of your mother or father
the child of your aunt or uncle
vocab.ex: I have four cousins in Taraz.

vocab.def: having a husband or a wife
vocab.ex: My cousin is married and lives in Astana.

ex.q: She ___ watch television in the morning.

ex.a: My brother works at the airport.
Does your sister live with your parents?

a: Does her husband drive a taxi?

pairs: the man a woman is married to
the child of your aunt or uncle

ex.a: My sister has two children and she lives in Astana.

ex.text: This is my family. My father works at the station and my mother teaches at a school. I have one sister — she is a nurse. My brother is only nine, so he goes to school.

ex.instr: Say each verb out loud. Which ending do you hear?

speak.p: Describe two people in your family: what they do and where they live.
speak.model: My sister lives in Astana and she works in a bank. My brother studies at university.

speak.p: Say one thing somebody in your family never does.
speak.model: My father never watches television in the morning.

speak.p: Ask your partner three questions about their family.
speak.model: Does your brother live with your parents? How old is your sister? Is your cousin married?

rows.label: Where it goes
items: We are usually late for the first lesson.
He is often tired in the evening.

rows.label: Asking
items: How often do you go to the gym?

notes: The adverb goes before the main verb, but after the verb be: I usually walk, I am usually late.
never is already negative. Say I never eat meat, not I don't never eat meat.
every day, once a week, twice a month go at the end of the sentence: I swim twice a week.
One time is once, two times is twice, then three times, four times.

vocab.ex: I wake up before my alarm.

vocab.def: to eat your first meal of the day
vocab.ex: We have breakfast together on Sunday.
He takes a shower after the gym.

vocab.def: to go away from a place
vocab.ex: I leave the house at half past seven.

vocab.def: the meal in the middle of the day
vocab.ex: Lunch is at one in our office.

vocab.def: to get into bed to sleep
vocab.ex: The children go to bed at nine.

vocab.def: on some days but not on others
vocab.ex: Sometimes we eat out on Friday.
He never drinks coffee in the evening.

ex.q: We ___ late for the first lesson.
___ do you go to the swimming pool?
How ___ do you visit your parents?
He goes to the gym twice ___ week.

ex.a: I always take a shower in the morning.
She is never late for work.

ex.instr: Add always in the right place.
a: We always have lunch at one.

ex.instr: Add never in the right place.

ex.a: I usually leave the house at half past seven.

ex.text: My name is Dana. On a normal day I wake up at six and take a shower. I never have a big breakfast — just tea. I leave the house at seven and I am usually at work by eight.
ex.q: What does Dana have for breakfast?

speak.p: Describe your normal weekday from waking up to lunch.
speak.model: I wake up at half past six, take a shower and have breakfast. I leave the house at seven and I usually have lunch at one.

speak.p: Say three things you always do and one thing you never do.
speak.model: I always check my phone, always drink tea and always walk to the bus. I never go to bed before midnight.

speak.p: Ask your partner how often they do three things.
speak.model: How often do you cook? How often do you see your parents? How often do you go to the cinema?

rows.label: Time
items: at — clock times and night: at seven, at midday, at night
on — days and dates: on Monday, on 3 May, on Friday evening
in — months, years, parts of the day: in March, in 2026, in the morning

rows.label: Place
items: at — a point: at home, at work, at the station
in — inside something: in Almaty, in the room, in a taxi
on — a surface or a line: on the table, on the fourth floor, on the bus

rows.label: In sentences
items: The lesson starts at nine on Tuesday.
We meet at the station in the morning.
She lives in Astana, on Abay Street.

notes: No preposition before every, this, next or last: every day, next Monday — not on next Monday.
at night, but in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening. That one is worth learning by heart.
British English says at the weekend; American English says on the weekend. Both are fine.
You sit in a car or a taxi, but on a bus, a train or a plane.

vocab.def: on all days, without a break
vocab.ex: She checks her email every day.
We visit my parents at the weekend.
The market is busy in the morning.
This street is quiet at night.
I have a Spanish lesson once a week.

vocab.def: any day from Monday to Friday
vocab.ex: On a weekday I start at eight.
We stop for lunch at midday.

vocab.def: the hours when you are not working
vocab.ex: In my free time I play the guitar.

ex.q: We have a meeting ___ Monday morning.
She works ___ a bank in the centre.
Our office is ___ the fourth floor.

ex.a: We meet at the station in the morning.
I go to the swimming pool once a week.

ex.q: I see my parents on every Sunday.
a: I see my parents every Sunday.

ex.q: The shop opens at the morning.
a: The shop opens in the morning.

pairs: any day from Monday to Friday

ex.a: We meet at the station at midday on Saturday.

ex.text: The shop opens at nine in the morning and closes at eight in the evening. On Sunday it opens late, at eleven, and closes at six.
ex.q: When does the shop open on Sunday?

speak.p: Say when you do three things, using at, on and in.
speak.model: I start work at eight in the morning. I have a lesson on Tuesday. In August I go to the mountains.

speak.p: Describe your weekend: what you do and when.
speak.model: At the weekend I get up late. On Saturday I meet friends in the centre, and on Sunday I stay at home.

speak.p: Say where three things in this room are.
speak.model: The books are on the table, my bag is on the floor and my phone is in my pocket.

test.q: She ___ drinks coffee in the evening.
The lesson starts ___ half past eight.

test.a: We always have lunch at one.

test.q: They watch television in the evening.
a: She watches television in the evening.

test.instr: Add never in the right place.
a: He is never late for work.

pairs: the child of your aunt or uncle
